LLC DISSOLUTION AND CANCELLATION
Prepared for Acme Ventures, LLC

RECITALS — DISSOLUTION AND WINDING UP
Acme Ventures, LLC was dissolved effective September 1, 2026, based on Unanimous vote of the members. This document records the winding up of Acme Ventures, LLC's affairs and the filing that formally cancels Acme Ventures, LLC's existence with the California Secretary of State. It addresses the statutory winding-up and cancellation process itself — a separate matter from whatever dissolution triggers and buyout terms appear in Acme Ventures, LLC's own operating agreement, which govern only when and how dissolution happens under the operating agreement's own terms, not how the company's existence is actually wound up and canceled with the state.

WHO CONDUCTS THE WINDING UP
Once an LLC is dissolved, state law puts someone in charge of winding up its affairs by default: the managers who did not wrongfully cause the dissolution, or if there are none, the members, or if there are none of those either, the person or a majority of the people who signed the articles of organization. Whoever ends up in that role must give written notice, by mail, of the start of winding up to every known creditor and claimant whose address appears in the company's own records. If a court instead orders the winding up — on a manager's, member's, or three-or-more-creditors' petition — the court's decree controls who does it. Absent a contrary provision in the articles of organization or a written operating agreement, the people conducting the winding up are entitled to reasonable compensation for doing so.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The managers who have not wrongfully dissolved the limited liability company, or, if none, the members, or, if none, the person or a majority of the persons signing the articles of organization, may wind up the affairs of the limited liability company, unless the dissolution occurs pursuant to Section 17707.03, in which event the winding up shall be conducted in accordance with the decree of dissolution. The persons winding up the affairs of the limited liability company shall give written notice of the commencement of winding up by mail to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the records of the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.04(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default winding-up authority and creditor notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.04.)
  "Except as otherwise provided in the articles of organization or a written operating agreement, the persons winding up the affairs of the limited liability company pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reasonable compensation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.04(c), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, compensation for winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.04.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who conducts an LLC's winding up by default and what notice duty attaches — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This document doesn't identify who is actually conducting a given LLC's winding up, or confirm that the right people signed the notices — that's a matter of fact for the company's own records, not something this statute settles on its own. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.04, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

PRIORITY ORDER FOR DISTRIBUTING REMAINING ASSETS
Once an LLC's known debts and liabilities have been paid or adequately provided for — including debts owed to members who are themselves creditors of the company — state law sets a specific default order for distributing whatever assets remain, unless the articles of organization or a written operating agreement says otherwise: first, to members to satisfy any liabilities for distributions the company already owed them; second, to members for the return of their capital contributions; and only after that, to members in the proportions in which they otherwise share in distributions. If the winding up is happening through a court proceeding or under court supervision, no distribution can be made until any court-ordered period for creditors to present claims has expired.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as otherwise provided in the articles of organization or the written operating agreement, after determining that all the known debts and liabilities of a limited liability company in the process of winding up, including, without limitation, debts and liabilities to members who are creditors of the limited liability company, have been paid or adequately provided for, the remaining assets shall be distributed among the members according to their respective rights and preferences as follows: (1) To members in satisfaction of liabilities for distributions pursuant to Sections 17704.04, 17704.05, and 17704.06. (2) To members of the limited liability company for the return of their contributions. (3) To members in the proportions in which those members share in distributions."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.05(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default distribution priority on winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.05.)
  "If the winding up is by court proceeding or subject to court supervision, the distribution shall not be made until after the expiration of any period for the presentation of claims that has been prescribed by order of the court."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.05(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, distribution timing when winding up is court-supervised (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.05.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default priority order for distributing an LLC's remaining assets on winding up — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This order applies only 'except as otherwise provided' in the articles of organization or a written operating agreement — the company's own governing documents can set a different order, and this document doesn't say whether a given LLC's documents do that. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.05, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

THE CERTIFICATE OF DISSOLUTION AND CERTIFICATE OF CANCELLATION
Formally ending an LLC's existence with the California Secretary of State generally takes two filings. First, on dissolution, the managers — or, if the 90-consecutive-days-with-no-members event is what triggered dissolution, whoever is conducting the winding up — must sign and file a certificate of dissolution stating the LLC's name, its Secretary of State file number, and which statutory dissolution event actually triggered it. Second, once winding up is complete and assets have been distributed, that same person must sign and file a certificate of cancellation of articles of organization, which must state the LLC's name and file number, that a final franchise or annual tax return has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board, and that filing the certificate cancels the LLC and ends its powers, rights, and privileges. If dissolution happened by the vote of all the members and the certificate of cancellation itself includes a statement saying so, a separate certificate of dissolution is not required — the two filings can merge into one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(1) The managers shall sign and cause to be filed in the office of, and on a form prescribed by, the Secretary of State, a certificate of dissolution upon the dissolution of the limited liability company pursuant to this article unless the event causing the dissolution is that specified in subdivision (c) of Section 17707.01, in which case the persons conducting the winding up of the limited liability company’s affairs pursuant to Section 17707.04 shall have the obligation to sign and cause to be filed the certificate of dissolution. (2) The certificate of dissolution shall set forth all of the following: (A) The name of the limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number. (B) Any other information the persons filing the certificate of dissolution determine to include. (C) The event listed in Section 17707.01 causing dissolution. (3) If a dissolution pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 17707.01 is made by the vote of all of the members and a statement to that effect is added to the certificate of cancellation of articles of organization pursuant to subdivision (b), the separate filing of a certificate of dissolution pursuant to this subdivision is not required."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the certificate of dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.08.)
  "(b) (1) The managers shall sign and cause to be filed in the office of, and on a form prescribed by, the Secretary of State, a certificate of cancellation of articles of organization upon the completion of the winding up of the affairs of the limited liability company pursuant to Section 17707.04 and distribution of its assets pursuant to Section 17707.05... (2) The certificate of cancellation of articles of organization shall set forth all of the following: (A) The name of the limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number. (B) That a final franchise tax return, as described by Section 23332 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, or a final annual tax return, as described by Section 17947 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board... (C) That upon the filing of the certificate of cancellation, except as provided in Section 17707.06, the limited liability company shall be canceled and its powers, rights, and privileges shall cease... (c) Upon filing a certificate of cancellation pursuant to subdivision (b), except as provided in Section 17707.06, a limited liability company shall be canceled and its powers, rights, and privileges shall cease."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08(b)-(c), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the certificate of cancellation and its effect (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.08.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual two-filing cancellation mechanism and what each filing must contain — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not a claim that every state uses a two-document process like this one. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones. A narrow exception to 'powers, rights, and privileges cease' on cancellation is addressed separately in this document, in the clause on continued existence after cancellation.

LIMITED EXISTENCE AFTER CANCELLATION
Filing the certificate of cancellation does not erase an LLC out of existence entirely. State law lets a canceled LLC continue to exist afterward, but only for a narrow set of purposes: winding up its affairs, prosecuting or defending lawsuits by or against it in order to collect and pay off what it owes, disposing of and conveying its property, and collecting and dividing its remaining assets — it cannot continue conducting business beyond what winding up actually requires. No lawsuit involving the LLC is dismissed just because a certificate of cancellation was filed while the case was pending. And if an asset gets missed during winding up, it does not disappear — it stays with the canceled LLC for whoever is entitled to it, to be used first to pay off any liabilities the company still owes, with anything left over going to the members.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A limited liability company that has filed a certificate of cancellation nevertheless continues to exist for the purpose of winding up its affairs, prosecuting and defending actions by or against it in order to collect and discharge obligations, disposing of and conveying its property, and collecting and dividing its assets. A limited liability company shall not continue business except so far as necessary for its winding up. (b) No action or proceeding to which a limited liability company is a party abates by the filing of a certificate of cancellation for the limited liability company or by reason of proceedings for its winding up and dissolution."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06(a)-(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, continued existence for winding-up purposes after cancellation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.06.)
  "Any assets inadvertently or otherwise omitted from the winding up continue in the canceled limited liability company for the benefit of the persons entitled to those assets upon cancellation and on realization shall be used to discharge unsatisfied liabilities, if any, known to the company, and any excess shall be distributed to the members."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06(c), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, assets omitted from winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.06.)
  Known gap: This corrects a framing this research started with: the relevant statute does not say an LLC's existence continues for limited purposes 'until' cancellation is filed. Verified directly, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06 says the opposite — the LLC's existence becomes limited to specific enumerated purposes starting after a certificate of cancellation is filed, not before it. Before cancellation (while merely dissolved and winding up), the company has not yet lost its powers, rights, and privileges under § 17707.08(c); those cease on cancellation, subject to this narrower continued-existence carve-out. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine post-cancellation continued-existence rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

THE SHORT-FORM CANCELLATION OPTION
California law provides a separate, simplified cancellation path for an LLC that meets a specific, narrow set of conditions, letting it skip the certificate-of-dissolution-then-certificate-of-cancellation sequence described elsewhere in this document. To use it, all of the following must be true: the LLC has not conducted any business at all since its articles of organization were filed; the certificate of cancellation is filed within 12 months of that filing date; the LLC has no debts or other liabilities, apart from the requirement that a final franchise or annual tax return be filed with the Franchise Tax Board; the LLC's known assets, if it has any, have already been distributed to whoever is entitled to them, or it never acquired any known assets in the first place; 50% or more of the voting interests of the managers (or, if there are none, the members, or if there are neither, the person or persons who signed the articles of organization) voted to dissolve; and, if the LLC took in any payments from investors in exchange for an interest, those payments have been returned to those investors. If all of that is true, the relevant people may execute and file a single certificate of cancellation without a separate certificate of dissolution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this title, if a domestic limited liability company has not conducted any business, 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the members, or, if there are no members, 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the managers, if any, or if no members or managers, the person or 50 percent or more of the persons signing the articles of organization, may execute and acknowledge a certificate of cancellation of articles of organization... stating all of the following: (1) The name of the domestic limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number. (2) That the certificate of cancellation is being filed within 12 months from the date the articles of organization was filed. (3) That the limited liability company does not have any debts or other liabilities, except as provided in paragraph (4). (4) That a final franchise tax return... or a final annual tax return... has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board... (5) That the known assets of the limited liability company remaining after payment of, or adequately providing for, known debts and liabilities have been distributed to the persons entitled thereto or that the limited liability company acquired no known assets, as the case may be. (6) That the limited liability company has not conducted any business from the time of the filing of the articles of organization. (7) That 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the managers or members voted, or, if no managers or members, the person or 50 percent or more of the persons signing the articles of organization, voted to dissolve the limited liability company. (8) If the limited liability company has received payments for interests from investors, that those payments have been returned to those investors. (b) A certificate of cancellation executed and acknowledged pursuant to subdivision (a) shall be filed with the Secretary of State within 12 months from the date that the articles of organization was filed."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.02(a)-(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, short-form cancellation eligibility and filing deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.02.)
  Known gap: This clause corrects two assumptions this research started with. First, the short-form cancellation eligibility rules are not found in Cal. Corp. Code § 17713.04 — verified directly, that section is a transition and applicability provision governing which LLCs the 2014 recodification (RULLCA) covers versus 'prior law,' with nothing about short-form dissolution or cancellation at all. The actual short-form provision, verified directly, is Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.02. Second, the eligibility test is not that the LLC 'commenced business within the last 12 months' — the verified statutory text requires the opposite: the LLC must have conducted no business whatsoever since filing its articles of organization, not merely recently-commenced business. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a genuine short-form cancellation shortcut exists with real, specific conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not a claim that any other state offers a comparable shortcut. This is a single statutory section (§ 17707.02); no additional independent source was found for this.

STOPPING THE ANNUAL LLC TAX ON CANCELLATION
Filing a certificate of cancellation (or dissolution) does not, by itself, stop the state's ongoing annual LLC tax. Under California's Revenue and Taxation Code, an LLC owes no further annual tax for a given taxable year only if it does all three of the following: files a timely final annual tax return with the Franchise Tax Board for the preceding taxable year; does no further business in California after that taxable year ends; and files a certificate of dissolution or certificate of cancellation with the Secretary of State within 12 months of the date that final return was filed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A limited liability company shall not be subject to the taxes imposed by this chapter for a taxable year if the limited liability company does all of the following: (1) Files with the Franchise Tax Board a timely final annual tax return for the preceding taxable year. (2) Does not do business in this state after the end of the taxable year for which the final annual tax return was filed. (3) Files a certificate of dissolution with the Secretary of State, pursuant to Section 17707.08 of the Corporations Code, or a certificate of cancellation with the Secretary of State pursuant to Section 17708.06 of the Corporations Code, before the end of the 12-month period beginning with the date the final annual tax return was filed."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947(a), Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, relief from the annual tax on timely final return and cancellation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17947.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a genuine, checkable tax-clearance mechanism ties the annual LLC tax to the cancellation filing — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not tax advice about any particular LLC's own filings or filing deadlines. This statute cross-references the certificate-of-cancellation filing under Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08 by name, which is independently verified elsewhere in this document. It also cross-references, by number only, Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.06 as an alternate certificate-of-cancellation provision and Rev. & Tax. Code § 18633.5's definition of a 'final annual tax return'; neither of those two specifically cross-referenced provisions was independently fetched and verified as part of this research, so their text is not relied on beyond what this section itself states. This is a single statutory section (Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947); no additional independent source was found for this specific tax-clearance mechanism.

WINDING-UP DECLARATION AND SIGNATURES
The undersigned, on behalf of Acme Ventures, LLC, declare the following: Acme Ventures, LLC's known debts and liabilities have been paid or adequately provided for; Acme Ventures, LLC's known remaining assets, if any, have been distributed to the persons entitled to them, or Acme Ventures, LLC acquired no known assets; and a final tax return for Acme Ventures, LLC has been or will be filed with the California Franchise Tax Board.

☐ Acme Ventures, LLC meets the short-form cancellation conditions described above and will be canceled by filing a single certificate of cancellation.
☐ Acme Ventures, LLC does not meet those conditions, and a certificate of dissolution will be filed together with (or before) a certificate of cancellation.

Signed:

_______________________________ Date: _______________
_______________________________ Date: _______________
(Add additional signature lines as needed.)

citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this title, if a domestic limited liability company has not conducted any business, 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the members, or, if there are no members, 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the managers, if any, or if no members or managers, the person or 50 percent or more of the persons signing the articles of organization, may execute and acknowledge a certificate of cancellation of articles of organization... stating all of the following: (1) The name of the domestic limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number. (2) That the certificate of cancellation is being filed within 12 months from the date the articles of organization was filed. (3) That the limited liability company does not have any debts or other liabilities, except as provided in paragraph (4). (4) That a final franchise tax return... or a final annual tax return... has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board... (5) That the known assets of the limited liability company remaining after payment of, or adequately providing for, known debts and liabilities have been distributed to the persons entitled thereto or that the limited liability company acquired no known assets, as the case may be. (6) That the limited liability company has not conducted any business from the time of the filing of the articles of organization. (7) That 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the managers or members voted, or, if no managers or members, the person or 50 percent or more of the persons signing the articles of organization, voted to dissolve the limited liability company. (8) If the limited liability company has received payments for interests from investors, that those payments have been returned to those investors. (b) A certificate of cancellation executed and acknowledged pursuant to subdivision (a) shall be filed with the Secretary of State within 12 months from the date that the articles of organization was filed.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause corrects two assumptions this research started with. First, the short-form cancellation eligibility rules are not found in Cal. Corp. Code § 17713.04 — verified directly, that section is a transition and applicability provision governing which LLCs the 2014 recodification (RULLCA) covers versus 'prior law,' with nothing about short-form dissolution or cancellation at all. The actual short-form provision, verified directly, is Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.02. Second, the eligibility test is not that the LLC 'commenced business within the last 12 months' — the verified statutory text requires the opposite: the LLC must have conducted no business whatsoever since filing its articles of organization, not merely recently-commenced business. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a genuine short-form cancellation shortcut exists with real, specific conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not a claim that any other state offers a comparable shortcut. This is a single statutory section (§ 17707.02); no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Filing a certificate of cancellation (or dissolution) does not, by itself, stop the state's ongoing annual LLC tax. Under California's Revenue and Taxation Code, an LLC owes no further annual tax for a given taxable year only if it does all three of the following: files a timely final annual tax return with the Franchise Tax Board for the preceding taxable year; does no further business in California after that taxable year ends; and files a certificate of dissolution or certificate of cancellation with the Secretary of State within 12 months of the date that final return was filed.

citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, relief from the annual tax on timely final return and cancellation
citations.quote: A limited liability company shall not be subject to the taxes imposed by this chapter for a taxable year if the limited liability company does all of the following: (1) Files with the Franchise Tax Board a timely final annual tax return for the preceding taxable year. (2) Does not do business in this state after the end of the taxable year for which the final annual tax return was filed. (3) Files a certificate of dissolution with the Secretary of State, pursuant to Section 17707.08 of the Corporations Code, or a certificate of cancellation with the Secretary of State pursuant to Section 17708.06 of the Corporations Code, before the end of the 12-month period beginning with the date the final annual tax return was filed.

This statute cross-references the certificate-of-cancellation filing under Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08 by name, which is independently verified elsewhere in this document. It also cross-references, by number only, Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.06 as an alternate certificate-of-cancellation provision and Rev. & Tax. Code § 18633.5's definition of a 'final annual tax return'; neither of those two specifically cross-referenced provisions was independently fetched and verified as part of this research, so their text is not relied on beyond what this section itself states. This is a single statutory section (Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947); no additional independent source was found for this specific tax-clearance mechanism.
